payload.answer: Two readings, and the spec must pick one explicitly rather than blur them. (a) ERGONOMIC: the existing concurrency is per-project and implicit -- there is no way to say 'run these three specific jobs now, together'. That is a real gap and a modest feature over existing machinery. (b) LITERAL SAME-BRANCH CONCURRENCY: several jobs writing one working tree at once. That is a genuinely hard problem, and the existing worktree-plus-integrate-lock design exists precisely to avoid it. If (b) is wanted, the spec must say what it buys that (a) does not, because the cost is high and the current design is a deliberate answer to the same question.

Add a way to run several named jobs concurrently -- e.g. `vibey work --parallel <id>,<id>,<id>` -- with a mechanism that stops them colliding while they work against the same branch. BEFORE designing any of that, resolve one question, because it determines whether this is a small feature or a hard one: vibey ALREADY runs jobs concurrently. Workers claim with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, hold per-kind leases, work in separate git worktrees under .vibey/worktrees/<cycle>/, and serialise the merge step behind an advisory lock (the 'advisory-locked integrates' in the architecture notes). So the honest first task is to state precisely what this command adds that `vibey worker -j N` does not.

A clear statement of what the command adds over `vibey worker -j N`; a coordination design that extends the existing lease/advisory-lock machinery rather than paralleling it; a test that actually forces contention (two jobs racing the same resource) and shows neither corrupts the other nor deadlocks; all 7 gates green.

[hard] Do NOT invent a second locking scheme alongside the existing advisory locks and leases. Two coordination mechanisms over the same resources is worse than either alone -- extend what exists or explain why it cannot be extended. [hard] Never block a worker on a human: any coordination must be lock-with-timeout or lease-based, never a wait for input. [hard] Every job stays idempotent under replay; a worker can die mid-parallel-run and another must resume safely. [hard] No deadlocks: if the design introduces any ordering between locks, state the total order that makes deadlock impossible. [hard] PostgreSQL is the only coordination substrate -- no Redis, no files-as-locks, no in-process-only state that dies with the worker. [hard] 100% branch coverage including the contention paths; concurrency code with untested contention is untested code. [soft] The 'chat mechanism' idea from the request is worth evaluating and probably rejecting: agents negotiating for resources is far more failure-prone than a lock, and it cannot be tested deterministically.

The scenario I can defend is narrow: an operator who wants THESE THREE specific jobs run now, together, as a named batch, with one consolidated result, instead of hoping the pool reaches them in some order. That is an ergonomics and observability gap, not a concurrency gap. If the investigation finds no scenario stronger than that, the honest deliverable is a small batch-selection command -- or a written recommendation NOT to build it. A spec that invents a justification for a feature is worse than a spec that declines one.
